fixes.explanation: False is right. A Levite, a man from the tribe of Levi, comes to that spot and sees the man, and “…he passed by on the other side.” (Luke 10:32). That's the second one to do it. The priest did the same thing a verse earlier (Luke 10:31).

The Sabbath and offerings are part of the Law (Exodus 20:8; Leviticus 1:2), but they aren't what the expert says here. He answers with loving the Lord your God with heart, soul, strength and mind. Then he adds loving your neighbor as yourself. Neither the Sabbath nor offerings came out of his mouth.

Those are good commands, friend, and they're in the Law too (Exodus 20:12, 16). But the expert doesn't quote them here. He quotes loving the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, strength and mind, and loving your neighbor as yourself. Both of his commands are about love.
Memorizing isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, “Do this and you will live.” (Luke 10:28). The word is do. Saying the commands is one thing, and doing them is what Jesus asks.
Yes, he asks, “And who is my neighbor?” The text says he wanted to justify himself (Luke 10:29). So the man who gave the right answer asks one more question. I think a lot of us know that feeling.

Prayer is a good question, but it isn't the one he asks. After Jesus says he answered correctly, the expert asks, “And who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10:29). That question is about the second command he quoted. It's the one that gets a story.
He doesn't ask that, friend. What he asks is, “And who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10:29). The text says he wanted to justify himself. Nothing in his question is about ranking laws.
No stopping to pray in this story. Jesus says that when the priest saw the man, “…he passed by on the other side.” (Luke 10:31). Prayer isn't mentioned. Passing by is what Jesus says he did.
The Levite passes by. Jesus says that when he came to that spot and saw the man, “…he passed by on the other side.” (Luke 10:32). That's what the priest did too (Luke 10:31). So the answer is False.
He goes right to him. The Samaritan, a man from Samaria, has compassion, then “…went to him and bandaged his wounds…” (Luke 10:34). The compassion comes first, and then he goes to the man.

Calling out for help isn't what Jesus says. The Samaritan, a man from Samaria, “…went to him and bandaged his wounds…” (Luke 10:34). Jesus doesn't mention him calling for anyone. He goes to the man and bandages him.
That's it. The Samaritan “…put him on his own animal…” (Luke 10:34). It's his own animal, not somebody else's. I think that's a generous thing to share.
No carrying on his back here. Jesus says the Samaritan “…put him on his own animal…” (Luke 10:34). Carrying the man on his back isn't mentioned. The animal is how the man gets to the inn.

Finding out who did it isn't what he says, friend. The Samaritan tells the innkeeper, “Take care of him…” and says he'll repay any additional expense when he returns (Luke 10:35). Jesus doesn't mention the robbers in what he says. Everything he says to the innkeeper is about the man's care.
